source.title: Meek Models Shall Inherit the Earth
source.authors: Hans Gundlach; Jayson Lynch; Neil C. Thompson

record.tranche_reason: The paper fits benchmark performance to inferred pretraining loss and models downstream-task performance from that fit, conceptually testing V6. It does not independently test the underlying training-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper uses Chinchilla-like scaling laws as assumptions in its training- and inference-cost models; those modeled loss differences are not independent tests of V1–V3. Figure 2's MMLU-to-inferred-loss fit and Figure 3's derived benchmark-performance curves bear on V6. Figure 5 reports an empirical MMLU-Pro gap across inference-price groups, but does not directly test any listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a strategic model on assumed Chinchilla and Kaplan loss-compute laws (eq. 1–3, 11–12). It never measures loss scaling. Its one empirical link to scaling, a sigmoid fit of MMLU to loss (Fig. 2), serves as a translation tool for the model. The loss there is inferred from parameters and data via Chinchilla, using Owen [2024] data. The text reports no coefficients, goodness of fit or out-of-sample check, so the fit cannot show whether downstream performance is predictable. Figures 1, 3, 4 and 6–10 are model outputs, not measurements. Figure 5 measures capability gaps across price tiers, not scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. Under current next-token scaling practices, diminishing returns to compute mean frontier models' advantage over fixed-budget 'meek' models peaks and then shrinks. The gap closes faster for inference budgets, and the authors draw governance implications, e.g. compute thresholds may not suffice. They caveat that RL, synthetic data and adversarial settings may break this. They also note their own empirical data (Fig. 5) is inconclusive.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the original loss-scaling sweeps or fit compute-optimal allocations. It assumes Chinchilla-like scaling in a theoretical inequality model and separately fits benchmark performance to inferred loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The modeled downstream results depend on the MMLU sigmoid fit and its 80% ceiling; the authors state that a higher ceiling would change the performance-gap relationship.

fits_no_version.finding: The MMLU-Pro gap between the best overall model and the best model priced at $0.5–$1 per 1M tokens is described as inconclusive. It is possibly constant or diverging by parameter count. The largest gap, in 2023–2024, falls outside the training-based forecast.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capability gaps between frontier and fixed-inference-budget models converge over time as diminishing returns to scale predict.

record.problems: The loss-to-MMLU analysis uses loss inferred from parameter counts and cited Chinchilla scaling laws rather than directly measured held-out loss. The text gives no sigmoid fit coefficients, uncertainty estimates, or out-of-sample validation. The authors describe the commercial-model data as sparse and inconclusive and parameter count as a very rough proxy for training compute.

untested.parts: Assumed via Chinchilla/Kaplan coefficients; no loss sweeps.
No extrapolation from small to large runs is tested.
Chinchilla-optimal training is assumed; allocation is not fitted.
Only a citation (Zhai et al. vision transformers); no test.
The MMLU–loss sigmoid fit is shown only as a figure, with no fit quality or predictive validation. Loss is inferred, not measured.
Model sensitivity to Kaplan vs Chinchilla exponents is explored theoretically (inflection time about 10 years with Kaplan). This is not an empirical test of fit-dependence.

missing.what: Sigmoid fit coefficients, goodness of fit and number of models for MMLU vs inferred loss. These are needed to judge whether it bears on V6.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theoretical and policy paper that takes scaling laws as inputs. The only empirical scaling-adjacent element (Fig. 2) reanalyses Owen [2024] with loss computed from Chinchilla formulas. That makes the analysis circular as a test of loss-based predictability, and it is unquantified in the text. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The paper assumes Chinchilla-like loss scaling; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
No small-run fits are evaluated against much larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or independently fitted parameter/token allocation is reported.
No architecture-depth or width comparison is reported.
No new modality or training regime is tested.
The MMLU fit uses loss inferred from parameter data and Chinchilla scaling, rather than directly measured held-out loss; no out-of-sample predictive test is reported.
The paper does not test how fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation vary with fitting choices, nor whether measured loss curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: Models in Owen [2024] dataset (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit MMLU benchmark performance to loss inferred from model parameters using Chinchilla scaling laws.
rows.measure: MMLU benchmark performance as a function of inferred loss; sigmoid fit
rows.note: The authors report making an updated sigmoid fit and describe its translated performance dynamics. No fit coefficients or predictive validation are stated.
rows.check: The state 'observed' is unsupported. The text only says 'we make an updated sigmoid fit'. It gives no coefficients, fit quality or residuals. Loss is inferred via Chinchilla from parameters and data, not measured, so this is effectively MMLU vs compute (Owen's own result). The value cannot be read.

rows.subject: Modeled p-step benchmark tasks (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Apply the fitted MMLU-performance relation to a task requiring p successful benchmark steps.
rows.measure: Modeled p-step benchmark performance and SOTA–meek performance gap
rows.note: This is a derived task-performance model, not a separate benchmark measurement. The text says longer multi-step tasks extend the period of large-model advantage.
rows.check: This should not be a row. It is a theoretical derivation (eq. 7): the fitted MMLU sigmoid is raised to the power p and applied to modeled SOTA/meek loss trajectories. Nothing is measured. The authors say the height difference is an artifact of the 80% fit ceiling.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: MMLU performance fit to inferred loss for the Owen [2024] model data
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a sigmoid fit linking MMLU performance with inferred loss; this is evidence of a fitted downstream-performance relationship, though not an out-of-sample prediction (r1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The modeled advantage for multi-step tasks depends on the MMLU fit and its stated 80% ceiling, so the result does not establish a general downstream scaling relationship (r2, r3).
